assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks turn atoms into a fundamental-physics instrument: the magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift of the trapping field, so thousands of atoms are interrogated at once with fractional uncertainty near 1e-18. This is precisely what I value: an unexpected, simple physical trick that opens a new precision regime, with uses (relativistic geodesy, tests of constancy of constants, a redefinition of the second) that follow from the science rather than driving it.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and led its early realisation; Ye's group demonstrated and then pushed the clocks to the current accuracy and stability frontier, and linked them to the frequency comb. The two-person configuration is clean. Others (e.g. Lemonde, Derevianko, Ludlow, Bloom) contributed but are outside the supplied credit and a three-person prize is not needed.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely reproduced: many independent laboratories (Japan, USA, Europe, China) operate lattice clocks, intercompare them, and agree at the 1e-18 level. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb, so this is a natural continuation and the timing is good.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to treat clocks as a continuation of the comb prize or as a separate discovery.
Jun Ye also appears in the ultracold-molecule candidate, which could create a credit-overlap question.
Priority between lattice clocks and single-ion clocks (Wineland's 2012 prize touched the latter) is not something I can verify here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Hubbard model in a clean, tunable setting: the superfluid to Mott-insulator transition, single-site resolved quantum gas microscopes, and a general platform for many-body physics. It answers a concrete question (what does a strongly correlated quantum system do) using controlled atoms, which is intellectually close to my own field and of broad impact.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and colleagues) supplied the theoretical proposal for the Bose-Hubbard model in lattices; Bloch's group delivered the Mott-insulator observation and a large part of the subsequent programme; Greiner made the decisive quantum gas microscope step. Cirac and Esslinger are also credited and have strong claims (Esslinger for the fermionic Hubbard realisation), so the cut to three is genuinely contested and I propose it tentatively.
assessment.maturity: Very well confirmed and reproduced by dozens of groups; the field is mature and its methods are standard. Recognition is timely, possibly somewhat overdue.
uncertainties: Allocation among five credited names is hard; Cirac, Esslinger or Hänsch's role could change the best trio.
Overlap with the 2001 and 2012 AMO prizes and with the trapped-ion and Rydberg candidates may split the committee.
Quantitative claims about quantum advantage in simulation are still being debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall and quantum anomalous Hall effects extend the 2016 topological-phase prize into a new class of materials with protected edge states and quantised transport. The theory (spin-orbit-driven topological order) and the experimental observation in HgTe wells and in magnetic topological insulator films give a complete arc from idea to measurement. I defer to condensed-matter colleagues on the finer points, but the result is clear, original and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Kane (with Mele) made the decisive theoretical proposal; Molenkamp's group observed the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal; Xue's group observed the quantum anomalous Hall effect. Mele, Hasan, Bernevig, Zhang and others have substantial claims and Zhang is deceased, so the trio is a compromise that leaves out some key theorists.
assessment.maturity: The quantised effects are reproduced and well understood, though the quantum anomalous Hall effect still requires very low temperatures and the technological promise has been slow. Timing is reasonable.
uncertainties: Credit among Kane, Mele, Bernevig, Zhang, Molenkamp, Hasan and Xue is disputed or incomplete.
Several separate discoveries (2D QSH, 3D topological insulators, QAH) are bundled here and might need distinct recognition.
I defer to condensed-matter members on materials-level confirmation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and the Berry geometric phase say that potentials and geometry have physical consequences in quantum mechanics even where no force acts. This is a fundamental statement about the structure of quantum theory that has been used throughout atomic, optical and condensed-matter physics (adiabatic evolution, molecular conical intersections, Berry curvature in band theory). That is the kind of deep conceptual discovery that I find compelling.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959) made the prediction; Bohm is deceased, so only Aharonov is available from the supplied names for that half. Berry's 1984 phase is a distinct and decisive contribution. Others, notably Ehrenberg and Siday earlier, and Simon, Pancharatnam and Longuet-Higgins, complicate the history. The two supplied names are a defensible pair.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally confirmed repeatedly (Chambers, Tonomura, and many mesoscopic and molecular tests), and conceptually stable for decades. If anything the recognition is late rather than premature.
uncertainties: Bohm's death and the pre-1959 Ehrenberg-Siday priority make attribution of the AB half awkward.
Two distinct discoveries are paired under one heading and the prize motivation would need careful wording.
Whether the committee regards the field as 'discovery' versus 'theoretical concept' is a question of taste.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Strongly interacting Fermi gases and the BEC-BCS crossover let experimenters tune a Feshbach resonance and move continuously from molecular condensates to Cooper-paired superfluids, connecting superconductivity, neutron-star matter and ultracold atoms in a universal regime. It is a clean demonstration of how nature behaves when interactions are as strong as the quantum limit permits.
assessment.attribution: Grimm, Salomon and Thomas each produced early decisive experiments (molecular BECs, pair condensation, universal scaling and thermodynamics). Deborah Jin and Rudolf Grimm, Zwierlein and Ketterle are central; Jin is deceased and Ketterle already holds a prize, which makes the exact configuration uncertain, and the Zwierlein group's vortex evidence is not in the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Well reproduced by many groups and measured with percent-level precision against theory, including the equation of state. Interpretation is stable. Slightly overshadowed by the earlier BEC prize, but still timely.
uncertainties: Jin's death and the absence of Zwierlein and Ketterle from the credited names complicate attribution.
Overlap with the earlier 2001 Nobel for BEC may reduce appetite for a second ultracold-atom prize in the same year as the lattice work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry uses the wave nature of massive particles for precision measurement of gravity, rotation and fundamental constants. It is a direct embodiment of quantum mechanics in an experiment, and it asks the question of how large an object can be in a superposition, which connects to where the quantum-classical boundary lies.
assessment.attribution: Bordé proposed the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer geometry; Pritchard demonstrated early matter-wave interferometers with atoms and molecules; Kasevich realised the gravimeters, gyroscopes and the large-baseline devices. Chu, who has already a prize for cooling, and Chapman, Rasel and others also made major contributions, so the credit is fairly distributed but not tidy.
assessment.maturity: Mature technology with absolute gravimeters in use and tests of the equivalence principle at high precision; reproduced across laboratories. Next-generation tests are in progress, so some aspects are still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with Chu's 1997 prize and with lattice clocks in precision measurement.
The more speculative applications, such as gravitational-wave detection, are not yet realised.
Credit for the first atom interferometers (Carnal-Mlynek, Keith-Pritchard, Riehle-Bordé, Kasevich-Chu) is divided.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade and programmable neutral-atom arrays provide a route to controlled many-body entanglement: a strongly interacting atom blocks excitation of its neighbours and a few hundred tweezer-held atoms are arranged at will. This brings together basic atomic physics, which I know well, and quantum simulation and computing, and has already revealed new many-body states.
assessment.attribution: The blockade proposal (Jaksch, Lukin, Zoller and collaborators), the first blockade and gate experiments (Browaeys, Saffman, Grangier) and the large programmable arrays (Lukin, Greiner, Browaeys) are each separate steps. Saffman has a legitimate claim and Grangier is not credited, so the trio is only one reasonable option.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly progressing; confirmation is solid for blockade but the claim of useful quantum computing is not mature. This is probably a few years early compared with the lattice and clock work.
uncertainties: Fast-moving field; important results of 2023-2025 may change who is seen as decisive.
Four credited names with overlapping roles; Zoller also appears in two other candidates.
Premature if the prize motivation relies on computation rather than on blockade physics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics places a superconducting artificial atom in a microwave resonator, reaching strong coupling and enabling dispersive readout and gates; it is the basis of most current superconducting quantum processors. It is a clean implementation of cavity QED ideas that I know from the atomic case.
assessment.attribution: Blais (with Girvin and coworkers) proposed the architecture; Wallraff, Schoelkopf and collaborators in the Yale group demonstrated strong coupling. Girvin and Devoret are not credited and the theory credit belongs partly to them; the 2025 prize on macroscopic tunnelling already honoured part of this lineage.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced worldwide and operational in commercial devices. Recognition might be premature relative to the 2025 prize, which has just covered adjacent work.
uncertainties: The 2025 prize overlap with Devoret, Clarke and Martinis weakens the case for a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon.
Girvin and Devoret are missing from the credited names, so the proposed trio may misstate decisive credit.
